ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Louisville, KY
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Louisville chemical, distillery, plant and river-terminal steel. Request a UT quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Louisville, Kentucky
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic technicians to Louisville and the Ohio River corridor for wall-thickness surveys and ultrasonic weld examination on process vessels, piping, storage tanks, boilers, structural steel and manufacturing equipment. You give us the component list, the code and the locations; we travel to your site, take the readings, and return a report your inspector can use. Request a UT quote for your Louisville site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Louisville

Louisville is a river city with an industrial west end. Along the Ohio River in the Rubbertown area, a cluster of chemical and specialty-materials plants grew up from refining and wartime synthetic rubber production, and it still makes resins, acrylics, formaldehyde-based products and other chemicals. Those plants run reactors, distillation columns, storage spheres and tanks, and piping carrying acids, solvents and monomers, so metal loss from corrosion and erosion is the standing question. Ultrasonic thickness readings at set locations answer it, and a trend line across outages tells the owner how much life remains.

The river itself creates more work. The Port of Louisville at Riverport, on the Ohio at mile 618, handles barge cargo such as petroleum products, chemicals, grain, fertilizer and building materials, with on-site rail linking to CSX, Norfolk Southern and a regional short line. Tanks, loading arms, dock structures, cranes and conveying equipment there all carry welded steel that corrodes in a wet environment. Elsewhere in the metro, automotive and appliance plants run large stamping, painting and assembly lines, and the UPS Worldport air hub supports a very large sorting and conveyor operation. Bourbon distilling adds a distinctive population of steam boilers, column stills, fermentation vessels and pressure piping.

  • Chemical-plant reactors, columns, heat exchangers, piping and storage tanks along the river
  • Boilers, steam headers and pressure piping at distilleries, plants and institutions
  • Terminal tanks, barge-loading piping and cranes at river and rail facilities
  • Structural steel and crane runways at automotive, appliance and logistics buildings
  • Bridge members and repaired welds on river-crossing and highway steel

What UT can and cannot tell you

Ultrasonic testing sends a pulse of high-frequency sound through steel and times the echo. For thickness, the time between the front surface and the back wall gives the remaining metal with good precision, which is why UT is the standard tool for corrosion surveys on vessels, piping and tanks. For welds, an angled shear wave sweeps through the joint and reflects from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, cracks and slag lines that sit inside the weld and cannot be seen from outside.

It has boundaries. Sound needs a clean, coupled surface, so heavy scale, flaking lining, weld spatter and rough cast finish must be dealt with first. Wet-process equipment with internal lining or deposits can return echoes from the deposit instead of the steel, and a technician has to recognize that. Stainless and dissimilar-metal welds, common in chemical service, scatter sound and need careful technique. Pitted wall is hard to gauge, because the beam may hit the shoulder of a pit instead of its bottom. A thickness gauge reports a number; it is the technician's reading of the waveform and a defined procedure that make the number trustworthy.

Codes and standards behind UT in the Louisville area

Chemical and refining owners typically manage pressure equipment under API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground tanks, using ASME Section V for the examination method. Article 4 of Section V covers ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 covers materials, and the contact pulse-echo thickness method appears in Article 23 as SE-797 and in ASTM E797. Under the API programs, the owner's authorized inspector is the one responsible for the inspection; Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports the data, including thickness at each condition monitoring location.

Process piping follows ASME B31.3, which sets ultrasonic provisions and acceptance in its tables. Structural welds in buildings follow AWS D1.1, whose inspection clause includes ultrasonic examination of groove welds, and steel bridge members follow AWS D1.5. For power piping at boiler houses, ASME B31.1 applies. Our ultrasonic testing guide introduces the method, and the Article 5 and thickness requirements explainer goes into calibration and recording rules.

How Kentucky regulates boilers and pressure vessels

Kentucky pressure equipment is governed by KRS Chapter 236 and the regulations in 815 KAR Chapter 15, administered through the Boiler Inspection Section of the state Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction. Those regulations reference the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and the National Board Inspection Code for construction, repair and alteration. For a Louisville plant this means a thickness survey on a registered vessel or boiler is more than a maintenance exercise: results feed the file the state inspector and insurer rely on, and a reading near minimum thickness may need a documented repair or re-rating.

Many sites also operate under OSHA process safety management, whose mechanical integrity element requires inspection and testing to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. Consistent thickness history, taken with the same technique from outage to outage, is the evidence of that practice. The numbers we record are laid out so they can be pasted into the owner's inspection database without translation.

How the ultrasonic examination is carried out

Thickness work begins with surface preparation and a grid. The technician picks a dual-element probe for corroded or rough steel, calibrates on a step block of matching material, and takes readings at marked locations so the next survey can return to the same spots. Where wall is thin or pitted, the waveform is watched to reject doubled echoes, and several readings are taken around each location so the minimum is recorded. Hot lines, such as steam piping, require high-temperature probes and couplant plus a velocity correction for temperature. Lined or coated equipment is examined with a technique that identifies the steel wall rather than the coating.

Weld examination uses an angle-beam probe at 45, 60 or 70 degrees chosen for wall thickness and joint design. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes, scanning covers the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where possible, and each indication is evaluated for amplitude, position and length against the code criteria. Calibration is verified at the start, during long jobs and at the end, and the checks are recorded so the readings can be defended.

Lined, coated and insulated equipment in the river corridor

Much of the steel in Louisville's chemical and beverage plants is not bare. Vessels carry rubber or glass-flake linings, piping runs under insulation that traps moisture, and tank floors sit on grade where corrosion starts underneath. Each condition changes how the survey is planned. Insulated lines need windows cut into the insulation at the chosen locations and resealed afterward, and the technician records which locations were opened. Lined vessels may be examined from the outside through the steel wall with a procedure that proves the back-wall echo belongs to the steel, not the lining. Where that cannot be shown, the owner decides whether to strip a small test patch.

Tank floors are a separate case: ultrasonic readings are possible only where the underside echo can be trusted and the plate is accessible, and a floor survey is normally agreed with the owner's tank inspection program in advance.

Who performs and approves the work

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians calibrate, perform and interpret; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. The employer certifies personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so you can ask for qualification records before work starts. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your plant needs a ultrasonic procedure written or a written practice reviewed, Level III consulting and written practice development are available as separate services.

What a UT report contains

Expect a report that stands alone. It names the equipment and component identification, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance basis, the instrument, probes, calibration blocks and couplant, and the technician and level. For thickness surveys it includes a sketch or isometric with the reading at each location, the nominal and required minimum thickness where supplied, and a clear flag for any location near or below the alert level. For weld work it lists every recordable indication by position, depth, length and amplitude with an accept or reject decision. Calibration checks, temperature of the surface and any limits on access are noted, because those details explain why a reading was or was not obtained.

Planning a UT job in Louisville

The Ohio Valley climate is humid. Summer heat and humidity make surface temperatures climb on tanks and piping and keep scaffold work slow, while winter cold and ice on river-front structures affect probe coupling and safe access. Plan hot-surface probes in summer and cold-weather couplant in winter. Chemical sites require badging, permits and hazard briefings, and some areas need gas monitoring; send technician names and site rules early. Planned outages at area plants, and the periods when distilleries and plants shut equipment for maintenance, are the natural window for taking thickness data because insulation is off and scaffolds are up.

Riverport and the rail yards add access considerations: dock safety, barge traffic and rail movements all restrict where and when work can happen. Tell us the gate procedures and any escort rules. We travel to your site with the equipment needed for the agreed scope, and Atlantis has no office in Louisville, so staging, power and lighting should be agreed before mobilization.

UT, MT and PT: the right method for the job in Louisville

Choose ultrasonic testing for wall loss and for flaws inside welds. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Louisville when the concern is a surface crack in carbon or low-alloy steel, such as a repaired lifting lug or a weld toe. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Louisville for stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals that chemical and food-grade processes favor. Combining methods is common: ultrasonic examination of a groove weld for volumetric quality plus a surface method on the same joint. The national ultrasonic testing page gives the broader service picture.

Training in-house ultrasonic technicians

Many plants prefer to own routine thickness gauging. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training based on SNT-TC-1A, with online theory and practice on the ultrasonic simulator, while hands-on work and the practical examination take place at your facility. Details for the area are on the Louisville NDT training page, and the eligibility checker shows how many hours each candidate needs.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Louisville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Louisville. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, terminal or structure for the agreed scope, bringing the instruments, calibration blocks and couplant the job requires.

faq.q: What is ultrasonic thickness testing used for at Louisville chemical plants?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall on vessels, columns, piping and tanks at set locations, so owners can track corrosion and erosion and plan repair or replacement before a leak develops.

faq.q: Can UT find defects inside a weld?
faq.a: Yes. Angle-beam ultrasonic examination detects planar flaws such as lack of fusion, cracks and slag within the weld volume, and indications are judged against the code or procedure acceptance criteria.

faq.q: Which standards apply to ultrasonic work on Kentucky pressure equipment?
faq.a: ASME Section V Articles 4, 5 and 23 give the methods, the owner's API 510, 570 or 653 program sets the plan, and Kentucky regulations reference the ASME code and National Board Inspection Code.

faq.q: Can thickness readings be taken through a lining or coating?
faq.a: Only with a technique and procedure that identify the steel back wall rather than the coating. Where that cannot be demonstrated, the lining may need to be removed locally before the readings are taken.

faq.q: Is UT possible on hot steam piping at a distillery or plant?
faq.a: Yes, using high-temperature probes, suitable couplant and a temperature correction, within the limits written in the procedure. Please tell us the operating surface temperature when requesting a quote.

faq.q: Who decides whether equipment can stay in service after UT?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector or engineer decides. Atlantis performs the examination, records readings and indications, and writes a report that gives that person the facts needed to decide.

faq.q: What should I send to get a UT quote for a Louisville site?
faq.a: Send the component list, material and nominal thickness, code, number of thickness locations or welds, surface condition, access limits and target dates. We reply within one business day with questions or a scope confirmation.

faq.q: Do you report thickness in a format we can load into our database?
faq.a: Reports list each location with its reading and identification in a clear table and sketch, which most owners can transfer into their inspection database or spreadsheet without rework.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train our staff in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. UT Level 1 and Level 2 courses give online theory and simulator practice, and your facility hosts the hands-on practice and practical examination under your written practice, since the employer certifies.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Louisville, KY
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection (MT) for Louisville plant, river-terminal, crane and fabrication welds and parts, reported to code. Request an MPI quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Louisville, Kentucky
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends magnetic particle technicians to Louisville and the Ohio River corridor to find surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Common jobs are weld repairs on process equipment, lifting gear and crane structures, river-terminal and rail components, press and tooling parts, and fabricated steel. Request an MPI quote for your Louisville site with the part list and code, and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection fits Louisville's industry

Louisville's industrial map is unusually varied for its size. In the west end and along the river, chemical plants and storage terminals operate vessels, tank shells and supports that see repair welding every maintenance season. At Riverport, barge-loading equipment, dock cranes, rail spurs and heavy handling gear work in a wet, corrosive atmosphere that breeds fatigue and weld-toe cracking. Big manufacturing plants make trucks, SUVs and household appliances, and every one of them runs presses, dies, overhead cranes, conveyors and welded fixtures where a cracked lug or hook can stop a line or injure a worker.

The air hub and the logistics buildings that surround it rely on very large welded steel conveyor structures and lifting equipment. Distilleries and bottling plants add steam boilers, pressure piping, and heavy steel tank supports. Bridge and highway steel across the river and the interstate system calls for crack checks at repaired details. Machine shops and fabricators around the city build and repair pressure parts and structural steel, where a magnetic particle check after grinding and rewelding is routine good practice.

  • Repair welds, nozzle pads and support attachments on chemical-plant vessels and tank shells
  • Crane hooks, shackles, lifting lugs and runway welds at plants and river facilities
  • Press frames, die components, shafts and gears checked for fatigue or grinding cracks
  • Conveyor and building structural welds, base plates and repaired connections
  • Bridge and highway steel details where cracks tend to start at welds

What MT detects and its limits

Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic metal: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic or ferritic stainless grades. The part is magnetized and fine iron particles are applied; any surface or slightly subsurface discontinuity creates a leakage field that gathers particles into a visible line. The method is quick, sensitive to tight cracks that the eye misses, and gives an immediate result the technician can mark and photograph.

It cannot inspect austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, brass or other non-magnetic materials, which matter a great deal in chemical and food-grade plants around Louisville; for those, liquid penetrant testing is the surface method. MT also loses sensitivity as a flaw sits deeper below the surface and will not find buried lack of fusion or wall loss, where ultrasonic testing is the answer. Crack direction matters because a flaw parallel to the field may not disturb it, and heavy paint, scale or weld spatter can mask indications or create false ones.

Governing codes and acceptance

Technique for magnetic particle examination of pressure equipment comes from ASME Section V Article 7. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 sets MT methods and acceptance for vessel welds, and ASME B31.3 calls for MT on piping where its examination rules require it, with acceptance in the code's criteria table. AWS D1.1 governs structural welds and AWS D1.5 steel bridge welds. ASTM E1444 is the practice behind many written procedures, and ASTM E709 is the method guide. Where your plant has its own approved procedure, we use it as long as it meets the code that governs the equipment.

Our Article 7 explainer covers yoke lifting power, the two-direction examination and light-level controls, and the complete MT guide is a general introduction for new buyers.

Kentucky's pressure-equipment framework

Kentucky regulates boilers and pressure vessels through KRS Chapter 236 and 815 KAR Chapter 15, enforced by the Boiler Inspection Section of the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction. These rules reference the ASME code and the National Board Inspection Code, so a repair weld on a registered vessel or boiler needs a documented examination before the inspector accepts it. Magnetic particle testing of repair welds is a frequent part of that documentation. Where Louisville owners follow API 510, 570 or 653 programs, the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection and Atlantis supplies the examination record. OSHA process safety management adds an expectation that mechanical integrity inspections follow good engineering practice, which a written MT procedure supports.

How a magnetic particle examination is performed

Preparation comes first: oil, loose paint, scale and slag are removed so particles can reach the surface. The standard portable tool is an electromagnetic yoke. The technician checks that it lifts the required test weight at the pole spacing in use, then examines each area twice with the yoke turned roughly ninety degrees, so cracks in any direction cross the field. Dry powder suits rough or warm field welds; wet visible or fluorescent particles offer higher sensitivity on machined parts and critical joints, with fluorescent work performed under controlled ultraviolet light in a darkened area. Prods are reserved for heavy sections where a yoke cannot reach, with care to avoid arc burns.

Field-strength indicators confirm the field is adequate and aimed correctly. Indications are classed as relevant or non-relevant, measured and compared with the acceptance criteria, then marked and recorded. After examination, parts bound for welding, machining or precision service may need demagnetization, and the residual field is checked with a meter to confirm it is below the limit stated in the procedure.

Weld toes, lifting lugs and press parts: what the inspector looks for

Different components fail in different ways, and the technician examines with that in mind. On welded attachments the usual crack starts at the toe where the weld meets the base metal, so the examination covers the toe and the heat-affected zone, not just the face of the weld. On lifting lugs and hooks the critical areas are the eye, the shank root and any place that has been ground or built up. On press frames, dies and shafts, fatigue cracks tend to start at sharp corners and keyways, and grinding cracks appear in a pattern that follows the grinding direction. Knowing these patterns tells the technician where to look first and how to orient the field.

That is why a brief description of the component's service helps when you request a quote. A hook that lifts the same load daily is a different case from a die that has been repaired and rehardened, and the procedure should reflect the difference.

Repairs on river-front and rail equipment

Equipment that works at the water's edge ages differently from equipment inside a building. Barge-loading arms, dock bollards, crane pedestals and rail-car handling gear are loaded from changing directions, soaked, frozen and thawed, and then repaired by welding. The weld toe on a repaired pad eye or the corner of a repaired crane pedestal is where cracks restart, so the examination covers the whole repaired area and a margin around it. Where the original crack was ground out, the technician examines the excavation before welding and the finished weld after, and the report keeps the two checks together.

Equipment in wet service can also carry a thin film of rust or marine growth that must be wire-brushed off before particles will behave. Sending a photograph with the quote request helps us plan the cleaning needed and whether wet or dry particles suit the surface.

The same approach applies to rail-served industrial buildings and manufacturing plants away from the river. Overhead cranes, hoists and lifting beams are normally examined on a periodic maintenance cycle, and a magnetic particle check after any weld repair or modification is the usual way to show the item is ready for a load test.

Qualification of the people doing the work

MT technicians work under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians carry out the magnetizing and read the indications, while an ASNT Level III signs off the procedure and reviews what is reported. The employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so qualification records can be provided on request. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your plant needs help writing or auditing an MT procedure, ASNT Level III consulting and written practice development are available as separate engagements.

What the report records

The report names the component and location, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance criteria, the equipment, the particle type and contrast or light levels, the yoke lifting-power check, and the technician and level. It records the surface condition, the magnetizing technique and directions, and the area covered. Each relevant indication is described by location, orientation and size, with an accept or reject decision, and a sketch or photograph locates it. A clean examination is recorded as carefully as a rejectable one because the file will be read later by an inspector, insurer or auditor.

Planning an MT job in Louisville

Louisville's humid summers put condensation on cooled equipment and can make particle suspensions behave unpredictably, while hot surfaces dry carrier fluids too fast. Winter cold and river-front ice slow work and make safe access harder. Outdoor fluorescent work needs a tent or shade at open yards and docks. Planned outages at chemical plants and manufacturing shutdowns are when most MT jobs concentrate, so send the weld or part list early, along with badge, permit and hot-work rules. Riverport and rail sites add dock safety and track-access restrictions to the plan.

We travel to your site with yokes, lighting, particles and calibration checks, and mobilize for the agreed scope. Atlantis has no office in Louisville, so tell us about power, lighting and cleaning support at the location.

MT, PT or UT for a Louisville job

Pick magnetic particle testing for surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel where speed and visibility matter. Pick liquid penetrant testing in Louisville when the metal is stainless or aluminum or the part is machined. Pick ultrasonic testing in Louisville for remaining wall or volumetric weld quality. See the national MT service page and the MT versus PT comparison if you are weighing options for a repair package.

Building in-house MT capability

Plants with steady weld repair work often train their own technicians. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A, with online theory and hands-on practice at your facility under your written practice. The Louisville NDT training page describes delivery for the area, and free practice tests help candidates prepare.

faq.q: What does MT find on Louisville plant steel?
faq.a: It finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks, laps and seams in ferromagnetic steel, including weld-toe cracks, fatigue cracks in lifting gear and press parts, and grinding cracks in machined components.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on stainless steel?
faq.a: Only on ferritic and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless, common in chemical and food plants, is not magnetic, so liquid penetrant testing is the surface method used for those materials.

faq.q: Why is the part examined twice in two directions?
faq.a: A crack is found best when it lies across the magnetic field. Examining twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees makes sure cracks in any orientation are detected.

faq.q: When is fluorescent particle testing used instead of dry powder?
faq.a: Fluorescent wet particles under ultraviolet light give higher sensitivity on machined parts and critical welds, while dry powder suits rough or warm field welds. The written procedure decides which technique is used.

faq.q: Which code governs MT on a Louisville pressure vessel repair?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 supplies the technique, with acceptance from the construction or repair code such as Section VIII Appendix 6 or B31.3, and Kentucky regulations reference the ASME code and NBIC.

faq.q: Does the part need demagnetizing after MT?
faq.a: Only when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or wear. The procedure states when demagnetization applies and the limit checked with a field meter.

faq.q: Can you examine crane hooks and lifting lugs?
faq.a: Yes. Hooks, shackles, lugs and runway welds are routine MT scopes. We follow your procedure or the applicable ASME, AWS or ASTM criteria and record the area covered and each indication.

faq.q: What happens if the surface is painted or rusty?
faq.a: Heavy coating, scale or rust must be removed in the examined area so particles can reach the steel. Thin, non-conductive coatings can sometimes be tolerated if the procedure demonstrates adequate sensitivity.

faq.q: How do I get an MPI quote for a Louisville site?
faq.a: Use the quote link on this page and send the part or weld list, code, surface condition, access rules and target dates. Our reply comes within one business day, with any questions about the parts and the access we need.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train our maintenance team in MT?
faq.a: Yes. MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses provide online theory, and your facility hosts the hands-on work and practical examination under your own written practice, since the employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Louisville, KY | Liquid PT
pt.description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for Louisville stainless, aluminum and carbon steel welds, castings and machined parts, reported to code. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Louisville, Kentucky
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes liquid penetrant technicians to Louisville and the Ohio River corridor to find surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps in welds, castings, forgings and machined parts, on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel. Dye penetrant inspection is the surface method for any clean, non-porous metal that magnetic particle testing cannot handle. Request a PT quote for your Louisville site and we reply within one business day.

Where dye penetrant testing is used in Louisville

The metals that Louisville industry prefers are often the ones magnetic methods cannot examine. Chemical plants along the Ohio River use austenitic and duplex stainless steels, nickel alloys and clad vessels to handle corrosive streams, so weld quality on piping, nozzles and heat exchangers is checked with penetrant. Food-grade and beverage operations, including distilleries, bottlers and ingredient plants, run stainless tanks, jacketed vessels, sanitary piping and copper stills, where a surface crack can harbor contamination or leak under heat cycles.

The manufacturing base adds another layer. Automotive and appliance plants maintain aluminum components, tooling, hydraulic parts and welded fixtures; cast housings and machined shafts need penetrant checks after repair or regrinding. Riverport equipment, from pump casings to valve bodies and stainless loading-line fittings, sees the same method. Power and steam systems at plants and institutions have stainless and alloy parts where socket welds, small-bore connections and valve seats are checked after maintenance.

  • Stainless and alloy piping welds, socket welds and small-bore branch connections
  • Stainless tanks, jacketed vessels and sanitary lines at food and beverage sites
  • Pump casings, valve bodies, cast housings and hydraulic components
  • Aluminum frames, tooling and fixtures from manufacturing plants
  • Repair welds on clad, overlay or non-ferrous equipment

What penetrant testing finds and what it cannot

Penetrant testing detects discontinuities that are open to the surface. A thin liquid enters cracks and pores by capillary action, and after the excess is removed a developer draws it back out so the flaw shows as a colored or glowing line. It works on any non-porous material, needs no electricity in the field and gives the technician a direct picture of the surface defect, which makes it well suited to small parts and awkward geometry.

It will not detect a flaw that does not break the surface. Buried lack of fusion, internal porosity and wall loss are outside its reach. Peened, ground or machined surfaces can smear metal across a crack and seal it, so those surfaces may need etching before the test. Porous surfaces hold liquid and produce a noisy background. Because the method depends on penetrant reaching the flaw, cleanliness is the main control: oil, paint, rust or residue from earlier tests can produce missed indications or false ones.

Codes and material controls

ASME Section V Article 6 provides the examination procedure for pressure equipment. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 gives methods and acceptance for vessel welds, and ASME B31.3 requires liquid penetrant examination of piping where its plan calls for it. ASTM E165 underlies many general-industry procedures, AWS D1.6 covers stainless structural welding, and AWS D1.1 allows penetrant as a surface check on carbon steel structures. The procedure we use names the penetrant type, removal method, developer form, dwell time and acceptance criteria.

For stainless and nickel alloys, materials must be low in halogens and sulfur so they cannot attack the metal; the product brand and lot are recorded in the report. Our Article 6 explainer sets out the main requirements, and the national penetrant testing page gives the broader overview.

Kentucky regulation and owner programs

Boilers and pressure vessels in Kentucky fall under KRS Chapter 236 and 815 KAR Chapter 15, administered by the Boiler Inspection Section of the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction. Those regulations reference the ASME code and the National Board Inspection Code, so a repaired stainless vessel or boiler component needs its surface examination documented. For owners using API 510 or 570 programs, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible and Atlantis provides the examination and the written record. OSHA process safety management expects mechanical integrity work to follow good engineering practice, and a controlled written PT procedure helps demonstrate that.

How the examination is done

The steps are cleaning, penetrant application, dwell, excess removal, developer, development time and interpretation. Surfaces are cleaned with solvent or detergent and dried completely; smeared metal from grinding may be etched to reopen cracks. Penetrant is sprayed or brushed on and left for the dwell time in the procedure, which grows longer on tight cracks and cold parts. Excess is removed with care: solvent-removable systems are wiped with lightly moistened lint-free cloth, water-washable systems are rinsed under controlled pressure so indications are not washed out. A thin even film of developer is applied and the surface is read after the development time stated in the procedure.

Visible red dye is typical in the field, and fluorescent penetrant under black light gives higher sensitivity on critical components. Standard penetrant procedures assume a metal temperature from about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; work outside that window needs a procedure demonstrated at the actual temperature using a comparator block. On stainless and nickel alloys, post-cleaning removes residue so no chemical stays on the surface.

Penetrant on stainless and copper-alloy equipment

Louisville's chemical and beverage sectors use materials that need extra care. On austenitic stainless steel, penetrant must be low in chlorides and sulfur, and any cleaning solvent and wipes must be compatible so no residue is left to cause stress corrosion cracking later. Copper stills and brass fittings are soft, and heavy wiping can smear the surface and close cracks; a gentle removal technique helps. On polished sanitary surfaces, over-cleaning with abrasives would damage the finish the owner paid to achieve, so mechanical preparation is limited and the technician relies on solvent cleaning.

When a surface is polished or electropolished, tell us before the job. The procedure can limit the products and cleaning steps so the surface finish and passivation survive the examination, and the report states what was used.

Weld repairs and castings: where penetrant finds problems

Penetrant results depend on where the technician looks. On a stainless pipe weld, cracks start at the toe, in the crater at a weld stop, and at the root of a socket weld where the fit-up leaves a notch. On a casting, shrinkage cracks and cold laps show at section changes and around risers that were ground off. On a machined shaft or valve seat, grinding cracks form a network that follows the grinding direction. Knowing these patterns lets the technician spend the dwell time and developer film where they matter, and write the report so the owner sees exactly where each indication sits.

The weld repair cycle benefits from penetrant at two points. After excavating a defect, the technician checks that the crack is gone; after welding and any required finishing, a second examination confirms the repair. When a repair has been ground flush, an etch step may be needed to reopen the surface before the final check, and the report records it.

Who performs and approves PT

PT technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician applies the materials and judges the indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so you can ask for qualification records before mobilization. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. For help with a penetrant procedure or a written practice, Level III consulting and written practice development are separate services.

The penetrant report

The report identifies the component and weld, material, surface condition and examination date, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance criteria, the penetrant type and method, the product brand and lot numbers, dwell and development times, and the surface temperature. Each indication is listed by location, length and shape, noted as linear or rounded, and judged accept or reject. A sketch or photograph shows where indications lie. Precleaning, post-cleaning and any etching are recorded, and the technician and qualification level are named so the record will stand up in an audit.

Planning a PT job in Louisville

Humidity is the Louisville variable. Water on a cold stainless surface from condensation, or damp air on a river-front pipe rack, can dilute penetrant and stop developer from drying properly, so the surface must be dry before work starts. Hot summer metal can flash solvent off before it does its job. In winter, a surface below the standard window needs a qualified low-temperature procedure or a heated enclosure. Tell us the expected temperature and exposure when you request the quote.

Chemical and food sites often require approval of every consumable, with safety data sheets and halogen certificates submitted ahead of time. Distilleries and beverage plants may have rules about aerosols and solvents near product areas. Our technicians travel to the plant with the penetrant system, comparator block and cleaning supplies the procedure lists. Atlantis has no office in Louisville, so staging, waste handling and who supplies lighting should be agreed before we mobilize.

Comparing PT with MT and UT in Louisville

Use penetrant testing when the material is non-magnetic, the surface is machined or cast, or the part is small and complex. Use magnetic particle inspection in Louisville for carbon and low-alloy steel welds where speed and sensitivity matter. Use ultrasonic testing in Louisville for the inside of a weld or the remaining wall. Many specifications call for penetrant on an alloy weld plus ultrasonic examination for volume. The MT versus PT comparison explains the trade-offs.

faq.q: What can liquid penetrant testing find in Louisville plants?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, porosity, laps and seams in welds, castings and machined parts, on any clean non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and nickel alloys.

faq.q: When should I choose PT over magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Choose PT when the metal is not magnetic, such as austenitic stainless or aluminum, or the surface is machined or complex. MT works only on ferromagnetic steel, while penetrant covers nearly any non-porous metal.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing detect flaws below the surface?
faq.a: No. Only discontinuities open to the surface are shown. Buried lack of fusion or wall loss needs ultrasonic testing, which can be combined with PT on the same weld when the code calls for both.

faq.q: Does the penetrant harm stainless steel equipment?
faq.a: Not when low-halogen and low-sulfur materials are used and residue is removed afterward. We record product brand and lot numbers so the material control can be checked by your quality team.

faq.q: How does humidity affect penetrant work in Louisville?
faq.a: Condensation or damp air can dilute penetrant and keep developer from drying evenly. The surface must be dry and within the procedure temperature range, otherwise the work is delayed or the procedure is qualified for conditions.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done on polished sanitary surfaces?
faq.a: Yes, with a procedure that limits abrasive preparation and uses compatible solvents so the finish and passivation survive. Tell us about the surface finish when you request the quote.

faq.q: What code covers penetrant work on Kentucky pressure equipment?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives the method, with acceptance from the construction code such as Section VIII Appendix 8 or B31.3, and Kentucky regulations reference the ASME code and National Board Inspection Code.

faq.q: Do you use fluorescent or visible penetrant?
faq.a: Both are available. Visible red dye suits most field welds and fluorescent penetrant under black light suits critical parts that need higher sensitivity. The specification and procedure determine which one applies.
